queue.tree_name: The Himalayan Cedar of the German Institute
queue.recognise: Beside the main house of the German Studies institute, a deodar listed for the shape of it rather than its size; the two registers give its trunk as five metres and as 3.3.
queue.story: Two official registers disagree about this trunk by nearly two metres. Italy's national list gives it as five metres around; the Lazio regional list, which is where the national one gets its Roman entries in the first place, says 3.3. Both are describing the same deodar standing beside the villa's main house, and neither has ever put a date on it. What the regional list does say is unusual: of the 65 monumental trees inside the comune of Roma, this is one of only three designated partly for architettura vegetale, vegetal architecture, the surveyor's term for a tree whose shape is itself the built object. Not its age. Not its girth. Its form. Cedrus deodara grows wild at 1,500 to 3,000 metres
queue.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the German Institute
queue.worth: closes a gap: this tree has no photograph at all

queue.tree_name: The Black Locust of the Ciutadella
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.3 metres round on a tree only 12 metres tall, stout where black locusts are usually thin. It stands in the parterre between the Passeig de Joaquim Renart and the Cascada.
queue.story: A trunk of 4.3 metres on a tree only 12 metres tall makes this the stoutest black locust in Barcelona and the only one the city has ever put on its register. Black locusts usually run up thin and fast and then fall over. This one went sideways and stayed, and it grows in the parterre between the Passeig de Joaquim Renart and the Cascada, the monumental fountain a young Gaudi worked on as a student assistant. How old it is nobody has established. The register's age column holds the words '100 anys' where a planting year should be, which is somebody's estimate written into the wrong box rather than a date anyone has checked, and the tree was only catalogued in 2024. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by what looks like a pine and is not: drooping grey green jointed twigs, and two trunks fused at the base that split about 90 centimetres up to a combined five metres round. It stands facing the Cascada.
queue.story: Everything about this tree says pine, and none of it is true. What look like drooping grey-green needles are jointed green twigs doing the work of leaves, and the real leaves are microscopic scales in rings at each joint, visible only if you pull a strand apart. Its relatives are the oaks and the birches, with not a single conifer among them. The river she-oak went into the ground beside the Cascada around 1894, six years after the Universal Exposition turned a demolished fortress into Barcelona's first public park, and it has thickened into two trunks fused at the base that separate about 90 centimetres up. queue.recognise: On the lakeshore path beside a bench: a pine whose trunk splits low into several stems, orange and peeling above, the branches layered flat over the grass and the lake behind.
queue.story:
A reader walking the boardwalk along Lake Ontario, east of the Beaches, stopped at this pine and sent us a photograph from its foot.

What stops you is the bark. Low down the trunk is grey and deeply plated, but where it divides the stems turn a warm copper orange and the thin skin flakes away in patches, the look of a Scots pine that has been shaped by wind. The trunk splits into three or four stems close to the ground, one of them sweeping out sideways over a bench, and the branches spread flat and wide, layered like the crown of an old pine in a Japanese garden. Behind it the lake runs out to a line of boulders along the shore.

We do not know its species for certain, its age or its girth
queue.name: Scots Pine in Toronto
queue.worth: the tree already has one: ship this only if it is better
